prompt: Light behaves both as a wave and as a particle. Which of its properties does the section say is explained best by treating light as a wave?

choices.text: Refraction as it passes into a new medium
Absorption of light by molecules in a sample
choices.why: Absorption is better described by treating light as particles, photons that each deliver a fixed energy. The wave model works best for refraction.

choices.text: Emission of light by atoms in a hot flame
choices.why: Emission, like absorption, is better described with the particle (photon) model. The wave model is best for refraction.

choices.text: The fixed energy carried by each photon
choices.why: Speaking of photons is the particle picture. The wave model best explains refraction, as light passes from one medium into another.

explanation: The section uses two models of light. Refraction, as light passes from one medium to another, is explained best by the wave model, while absorption and emission are better described by treating light as particles.

prompt: According to the section, what does electromagnetic radiation consist of?

choices.text: Oscillating electric and magnetic fields
A stream of tiny charged particles
choices.why: Light carries no charge. It consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that travel through space.

choices.text: Oscillating electric fields only, with no magnetic field
choices.why: There is a magnetic field too. The radiation is an oscillating electric field together with an oscillating magnetic field.

choices.text: Vibrations of the air or other medium it passes through
choices.why: That describes sound. Electromagnetic radiation needs no medium: its oscillating electric and magnetic fields travel even through a vacuum.

explanation: Electromagnetic radiation consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that propagate through space along a linear path at a constant velocity. In a vacuum that velocity is the speed of light, c.

prompt: How are the oscillating electric and magnetic fields of an electromagnetic wave oriented?

choices.text: Perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
Parallel to each other and to the direction of travel
choices.why: Neither field oscillates along the direction of travel. The two fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction the wave moves.

choices.text: Parallel to each other, both at right angles to the direction of travel
choices.why: The two fields are not parallel to each other. Each is perpendicular to the other, and both are perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

choices.text: Both along the direction of travel, pointing opposite ways
choices.why: Neither field points along the direction of travel. They oscillate at right angles to it and to each other.

explanation: In an electromagnetic wave the electric and magnetic fields oscillate at right angles to each other, and both are perpendicular to the direction in which the wave propagates.

prompt: How does the speed v of electromagnetic radiation in a medium such as water compare with its speed c in a vacuum?

choices.text: v is less than c
v is greater than c
choices.why: Light travels fastest in a vacuum. In any other medium its velocity v is less than c.

choices.text: v equals c in every medium
choices.why: Only in a vacuum does light travel at c. In a medium it is slower, although in air the difference is under 0.1%.

choices.text: v depends on the wave's amplitude, not the medium
choices.why: The amplitude doesn't set the speed. In any medium other than a vacuum, light travels more slowly than c.

explanation: In a vacuum electromagnetic radiation travels at c = 2.99792 × 10^8 m/s. In any other medium its velocity v is less than c; in water, for example, light is about 25% slower.

prompt: Why is c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s accurate enough for light traveling through air in most calculations?

choices.text: In air, light is less than 0.1% slower than in a vacuum
Light travels faster in air than in a vacuum
choices.why: Light is never faster than in a vacuum. The value works because in air v differs from c by less than 0.1%.

choices.text: Air has no effect at all on the speed of light
choices.why: Air does slow light slightly, but by less than 0.1%, too little to change three significant figures.

choices.text: The value of c is only known to three significant figures
choices.why: c is known much more precisely, 2.99792 × 10^8 m/s. Three figures are enough because air slows light by less than 0.1%.

explanation: In a vacuum c = 2.99792 × 10^8 m/s. In air the velocity v differs from c by less than 0.1%, so the speed of light to three significant figures, 3.00 × 10^8 m/s, is accurate enough.

prompt: Plane-polarized radiation has a single oscillating electric field and a single oscillating magnetic field. How does ordinary, unpolarized radiation differ?

choices.text: Fields in every plane perpendicular to its travel
An electric field but no magnetic field
choices.why: Unpolarized light still has both fields. The difference is that they oscillate in every possible plane perpendicular to the direction of travel.

choices.text: Fields oscillating along its own direction of travel
choices.why: The fields always oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel. In unpolarized light they do so in all such planes, not just one.

choices.text: Fields that point one way and never oscillate
choices.why: All electromagnetic radiation has oscillating fields. In unpolarized light they oscillate in all possible planes perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

explanation: Normally electromagnetic radiation is unpolarized: oscillating electric and magnetic fields are present in all possible planes perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Plane-polarized radiation keeps just one such pair.

prompt: In A_t = A_e sin(2πνt + φ), which describes the electric field of a wave, what does the phase angle φ account for?

choices.text: The field need not be zero at time t = 0
The direction in which the wave travels
choices.why: φ does not set the direction of travel. It shifts the sine wave in time, so A_t need not be zero at t = 0.

choices.text: The maximum strength of the electric field
choices.why: That is A_e, the maximum amplitude. φ allows the field to have a value other than zero at t = 0.

choices.text: The number of oscillations per unit time
choices.why: That is the frequency ν. The phase angle φ accounts for A_t not being zero at t = 0.

explanation: In A_t = A_e sin(2πνt + φ), A_e is the maximum amplitude and ν is the frequency. The phase angle φ accounts for the fact that A_t need not be zero at t = 0, where the field is A_e sin φ.

prompt: How does the section define the wavelength λ of electromagnetic radiation?

choices.text: The distance between successive maxima of the wave
The height of a maximum, the amplitude
choices.why: That is the amplitude, A. The wavelength is a distance along the wave: from one maximum to the next.

choices.text: The number of oscillations per second
choices.why: That is the frequency ν. The wavelength is the distance between neighboring maxima.

choices.text: The distance between a maximum and the next minimum
choices.why: A maximum and the following minimum are only half a wavelength apart. λ is the distance between successive maxima.

explanation: The wavelength λ is the distance between successive maxima of the wave. It is related to the frequency by λ = c/ν, so a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.

prompt: In which unit is the wavelength of infrared radiation usually given?

choices.text: Microns, μm (1 μm = 10^−6 m)
Nanometers, nm (1 nm = 10^−9 m)
choices.why: Nanometers are usually used for ultraviolet and visible light. Infrared wavelengths are given in microns, μm.

choices.text: Picometers, pm (1 pm = 10^−12 m)
choices.why: Picometers are far too small for infrared waves, which are millionths of a meter long. They are given in microns.

choices.text: Centimeters, cm (1 cm = 10^−2 m)
choices.why: Centimeters appear in the wavenumber unit, cm^−1, but infrared wavelengths themselves are usually given in microns, μm.

explanation: For ultraviolet and visible radiation the wavelength is usually expressed in nanometers (1 nm = 10^−9 m), and for infrared radiation in microns (1 μm = 10^−6 m). Infrared radiation is also often described by its wavenumber, in cm^−1.

prompt: On what basis is electromagnetic radiation divided into the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum?

choices.text: The kind of atomic or molecular transition it causes
The color the radiation appears to the eye
choices.why: Only the narrow visible region has colors. The regions are based on the type of atomic or molecular transition that absorbs or emits the photons.

choices.text: How fast each kind of radiation travels through a vacuum
choices.why: All electromagnetic radiation travels at c in a vacuum. The regions are set by the type of transition that absorbs or emits the photons.

choices.text: Whether the radiation is polarized or not
choices.why: Polarization doesn't define the regions. They are based on the type of atomic or molecular transition that gives rise to absorption or emission.

explanation: Frequency and wavelength vary over many orders of magnitude, so for convenience the spectrum is divided into regions based on the type of atomic or molecular transition that gives rise to the absorption or emission of photons.

prompt: What does the section say about the boundaries between the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum?

choices.text: They are not rigid, and regions can overlap
They are fixed exactly by international agreement
choices.why: The section stresses the opposite: the boundaries are not rigid, and neighboring regions may overlap.

choices.text: They fall at exact powers of ten in frequency
choices.why: The frequency ranges are rough guides. The boundaries are not rigid, and overlap between regions is possible.

choices.text: They are where the speed of light changes
choices.why: Light of every region travels at c in a vacuum. The boundaries are only approximate, and the regions can overlap.

explanation: The regions are a convenience. Their boundaries are not rigid, and overlap between spectral regions is possible.

prompt: When a molecule absorbs microwave radiation, between which kind of energy levels does it move?

choices.text: Rotational energy levels
Electronic energy levels
choices.why: Electronic transitions need much more energy, from visible and ultraviolet light. Microwaves cause transitions between rotational levels.

choices.text: Vibrational energy levels
choices.why: Vibrational transitions are caused by infrared radiation. Microwave photons change only the rotational state.

choices.text: Nuclear spin energy levels
choices.why: Nuclear spin transitions, studied by NMR, use radio waves. Microwave absorption gives transitions between rotational energy levels.

explanation: Microwave photons carry little energy, and absorbing them causes transitions between rotational energy levels. The section places the rotations of polyatomic molecules at 10^9 to 10^11 Hz, in the microwave range.

prompt: According to the section, what happens when a molecule absorbs infrared radiation?

choices.text: It changes vibrational level, with rotational changes too
It changes only its rotational level
choices.why: Rotational changes alone come from microwaves. Infrared absorption changes the vibrational level, accompanied by rotational transitions.

choices.text: It changes its electronic level
choices.why: Electronic transitions need visible or ultraviolet light. Infrared radiation changes the vibrational level, along with rotational transitions.

choices.text: It changes vibrational level while its rotation stays fixed
choices.why: The section says vibrational transitions are accompanied by transitions between rotational levels, so the rotational state changes as well.

explanation: Absorbing infrared radiation causes transitions between vibrational levels, accompanied by transitions between rotational levels.

prompt: Which kind of transition does the section link to the absorption of visible and ultraviolet radiation?

choices.text: Electronic, plus vibrational and rotational changes
Rotational only, with no change in vibration or electrons
choices.why: Pure rotational transitions come from microwave absorption. Visible and UV light cause electronic transitions, along with vibrational and rotational ones.

choices.text: Vibrational only, with no change in the electrons
choices.why: Vibrational transitions come with infrared radiation. Visible and ultraviolet photons have enough energy to change the electronic state.

choices.text: Changes in the spin orientation of the atomic nuclei
choices.why: Nuclear spin transitions use radio waves, in NMR. Visible and ultraviolet radiation gives electronic transitions.

explanation: Visible and ultraviolet photons carry enough energy to cause transitions between electronic energy levels. These are accompanied by simultaneous transitions between vibrational and rotational levels.

prompt: The section lists frequency ranges for different molecular processes. Which one does it link to 10^11 to 10^13 Hz, in the far infrared?

choices.text: Rotation of small molecules
Vibrations of flexible bonds
choices.why: The section puts vibrations of flexible bonds at 10^13 to 10^14 Hz, in the infrared. The far infrared is linked to rotation of small molecules.

choices.text: Electronic transitions
choices.why: Electronic transitions lie much higher, at 10^14 to 10^16 Hz, in the visible and ultraviolet.

choices.text: Nuclear spin flips in a magnetic field
choices.why: Nuclear spin transitions use radio waves, far lower in frequency. The section links 10^11 to 10^13 Hz to rotation of small molecules.

explanation: The section's ranges are 10^9 to 10^11 Hz (microwave) for rotation of polyatomic molecules, 10^11 to 10^13 Hz (far infrared) for rotation of small molecules, 10^13 to 10^14 Hz (infrared) for vibrations, and 10^14 to 10^16 Hz (visible and ultraviolet) for electronic transitions.

prompt: Which list puts molecular transitions in order of increasing frequency of the radiation that causes them?

choices.text: Rotational, then vibrational, then electronic
Electronic, then vibrational, then rotational
choices.why: This is the order of decreasing frequency. Rotational transitions need the lowest frequencies (microwave), electronic the highest (visible and UV).

choices.text: Vibrational, then rotational, then electronic
choices.why: Rotational transitions need less energy than vibrational ones: microwaves rather than infrared. The order is rotational, vibrational, electronic.

choices.text: Rotational, then electronic, then vibrational
choices.why: Electronic transitions need the highest frequencies, 10^14 to 10^16 Hz, above vibrations at 10^13 to 10^14 Hz.

explanation: Rotational transitions are caused by microwave and far-infrared radiation (about 10^9 to 10^13 Hz), vibrational ones by infrared (10^13 to 10^14 Hz), and electronic ones by visible and ultraviolet light (10^14 to 10^16 Hz).

prompt: What does the equation ΔE = E_u − E_l = hν say about a spectral transition?

choices.text: The photon's frequency is set by the gap between the two levels
The photon's frequency is the sum of the two levels' energies divided by h
choices.why: It's the difference, not the sum: hν = E_u − E_l, the energy of the upper state minus that of the lower state.

choices.text: The photon's frequency equals the upper level's energy divided by h
choices.why: Only the difference matters. ν = (E_u − E_l)/h, so the gap between the upper and lower levels sets the frequency.

choices.text: The photon's frequency is set by the lower level's energy alone
choices.why: The lower level alone doesn't fix the frequency. It is the difference E_u − E_l between the upper and lower levels that equals hν.

explanation: E_u and E_l are the energies of the upper and lower states. The photon's energy hν must equal their difference, so a larger gap means a higher frequency.

prompt: According to Table 13.1.1, which region of the electromagnetic spectrum does nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy use?

choices.text: Radio waves
Microwaves
choices.why: Table 13.1.1 lists microwaves for microwave spectroscopy and electron spin resonance. NMR uses the lower-energy radio waves.

choices.text: Infrared light
choices.why: Infrared radiation is used in infrared spectroscopy, to excite vibrations. NMR uses radio waves.

choices.text: X-rays
choices.why: X-rays are used in X-ray absorption and X-ray fluorescence. NMR uses radio waves, the lowest-energy region in the table.

explanation: Table 13.1.1 lists nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy under the absorption of radio waves, the lowest-energy region in the table.

prompt: According to Table 13.1.1, Mössbauer spectroscopy is based on the absorption of which kind of radiation?

choices.text: γ-rays
X-rays
choices.why: X-rays are used in X-ray absorption spectroscopy and X-ray fluorescence. Mössbauer spectroscopy uses γ-rays, the highest-energy region in the table.

choices.text: Ultraviolet light
choices.why: Ultraviolet light is used in UV/Vis spectroscopy. Mössbauer spectroscopy absorbs γ-rays.

choices.text: Radio waves
choices.why: Radio waves are used in NMR, at the low-energy end of the table. Mössbauer spectroscopy is at the opposite end, with γ-rays.

explanation: Table 13.1.1 lists Mössbauer spectroscopy as the absorption of γ-rays, the highest-energy radiation in the table.

prompt: In Table 13.1.1, fluorescence and phosphorescence spectroscopy are listed under which type of energy transfer?

choices.text: Photoluminescence
Chemiluminescence
choices.why: Table 13.1.1 lists chemiluminescence as a separate type, with chemiluminescence spectroscopy. Fluorescence and phosphorescence are under photoluminescence.

choices.text: Emission by thermal excitation
choices.why: Thermal excitation is the type listed for atomic emission spectroscopy. Fluorescence and phosphorescence are photoluminescence.

choices.text: Absorption
choices.why: Absorption covers techniques such as UV/Vis and infrared spectroscopy. Fluorescence and phosphorescence are listed under photoluminescence.

explanation: Table 13.1.1 lists fluorescence, phosphorescence and atomic fluorescence spectroscopy (UV/Vis), along with X-ray fluorescence, under photoluminescence.

prompt: According to Table 13.1.1, how is the sample excited in atomic emission spectroscopy?

choices.text: Thermally, by heating it
By absorbing X-ray photons
choices.why: That describes X-ray fluorescence, a photoluminescence technique. Atomic emission spectroscopy uses thermal excitation.

choices.text: By a chemical reaction
choices.why: Excitation by a chemical reaction gives chemiluminescence. Atomic emission is listed as emission after thermal excitation.

choices.text: By absorbing radio waves in a magnetic field
choices.why: That describes NMR, an absorption technique. Atomic emission spectroscopy excites the atoms thermally.

explanation: Table 13.1.1 lists atomic emission spectroscopy (UV/Vis) under emission after thermal excitation: the atoms are excited by heat and then emit photons.

prompt: According to the section, when is a spectroscopic measurement possible?

choices.text: When the sample changes one of the light's properties
Only when the sample emits light of its own
choices.why: Emission is one route, but absorption and other changes count too. What matters is that the interaction changes some property of the radiation.

choices.text: Only when the light passes through without any change
choices.why: If nothing about the light changed, there would be nothing to measure. A measurement needs a change in at least one property of the radiation.

choices.text: Only when the light is plane-polarized
choices.why: Polarization is one property that can change, but the light need not be polarized. A change in any property, such as energy or direction, can be measured.

explanation: Electromagnetic radiation is characterized by its energy, velocity, amplitude, frequency, phase angle, polarization and direction of propagation. A spectroscopic measurement is possible only if the photon's interaction with the sample changes one or more of these.

prompt: The section divides spectroscopy into two broad classes. What do all the techniques in Table 13.1.1 have in common?

choices.text: Energy is exchanged between a photon and the sample
All of them use visible light
choices.why: The table runs from γ-rays to radio waves. What the techniques share is an exchange of energy between photon and sample.

choices.text: All of them measure only light that the sample emits
choices.why: Many are absorption techniques, such as infrared and NMR spectroscopy. What they share is a transfer of energy between photon and sample.

choices.text: None of them change the energy of the light
choices.why: The opposite: in every one, energy passes between the photon and the sample, by absorption or emission.

explanation: Table 13.1.1 lists techniques in which there is a transfer of energy between the photon and the sample: absorption, emission after thermal excitation, photoluminescence and chemiluminescence.

prompt: Exercise 13.1.1 asks about a Balmer line of hydrogen with a wavelength of 656.3 nm. Using ν = c/λ with c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s and 1 nm = 10^−9 m, what is its frequency, in Hz? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e13.)
explanation: ν = c/λ = (3.00 × 10^8 m/s)/(656.3 × 10^−9 m) = 4.57 × 10^14 s^−1, or 4.57 × 10^14 Hz. This lies in the 10^14 to 10^16 Hz range of electronic transitions.

prompt: The gap between two molecular energy levels is ΔE = E_u − E_l = 3.313 × 10^−20 J. Using ΔE = hν with h = 6.626 × 10^−34 J·s, what is the frequency of the photon absorbed in this transition, in Hz? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e13.)
explanation: ν = ΔE/h = (3.313 × 10^−20 J)/(6.626 × 10^−34 J·s) = 5.0 × 10^13 Hz. In the section's ranges, 10^13 to 10^14 Hz is the infrared, where bonds vibrate.

prompt: An infrared absorption has a frequency of 1.2 × 10^13 Hz. Using λ = c/ν with c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s and 1 μm = 10^−6 m, what is its wavelength, in μm?
explanation: λ = c/ν = (3.00 × 10^8 m/s)/(1.2 × 10^13 s^−1) = 2.5 × 10^−5 m = 25 μm. Infrared wavelengths are usually given in microns.

prompt: Wavenumbers are often used for infrared radiation. Using ν̃ = 1/λ and 1 μm = 10^−4 cm, what is the wavenumber of infrared light with λ = 5.0 μm, in cm^−1?

Table 13.1.1 lists NMR spectroscopy under radio waves. An NMR spectrometer works at 600 MHz, or 6.00 × 10^8 Hz. Using λ = c/ν with c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s, what is the wavelength of this radiation, in meters? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: λ = c/ν = (3.00 × 10^8 m/s)/(6.00 × 10^8 s^−1) = 0.500 m. Radio waves are long: this one is half a meter, against micrometers for infrared.

prompt: The electric field of a wave is A_t = A_e sin(2πνt + φ). Take A_e = 4.0 (in any units) and φ = π/6, and use sin(π/6) = 0.5. What is A_t at t = 0?
explanation: At t = 0 the term 2πνt is zero, so A_t = A_e sin φ = 4.0 × sin(π/6) = 4.0 × 0.5 = 2.0. Because of the phase angle, A_t need not be zero at t = 0.

prompt: Combining E = hν, ν = c/λ and ν̃ = 1/λ gives E = hcν̃. Using hc = 1.986 × 10^−23 J·cm, what is the energy of an infrared photon with ν̃ = 3000 cm^−1, in J? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-19.)
